content:
Alex G (support): Jordan from Acme here — their app is seeing bursts of 429s and token-level slowdowns when they do load tests. They report it feels like throttling even though they have Dedicated capacity assigned.

Jordan (Acme): yes, we ramp from ~50 rps to ~800 rps for a couple minutes. Most of the responses are fine, but ~15% come back with 429 or take >2s to start streaming. No auth errors.

Alex G (support): thanks. I asked for request IDs and sample headers. Jordan — can you paste one failing request's response headers (x-request-id, x-redwood-rate-limit-*, x-redwood-instance)?

Jordan (Acme): here, two examples (scrubbed):

```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
x-request-id: rwd-req-0a1b2c3d
x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining: 0
x-redwood-rate-limit-reset: 167
x-redwood-instance-id: ded-42
content-type: application/json
```

and a slow one:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-request-id: rwd-req-0a1b2c60
x-redwood-instance-id: ded-42
x-redwood-kv-cache-hit: false
x-redwood-batch-id: batch-9
content-type: text/event-stream
```

Maria S (sre): interesting — remaining=0 suggests a rate/quota hit on that specific origin key. Dedicated usually has high per-second rate limits but there are two modes that can cause perceived throttling: global per-API-key quota exhaustion and batching/continuous-batching latency windows.

Sanjay P (eng): adding context: our continuous batching groups requests to maximize GPU utilization. Batches form up to max_batch_tokens or max_batch_latency_ms. Under large concurrent bursts, earlier small requests can get queued briefly to form a larger batch — that can show up as a small delay in start-of-stream. Also when KV cache is cold/invalidated we may have extra token compute for prefixes.

Alex G (support): Jordan, can you share the shape of the requests? Specifically: average prompt length, max tokens, concurrency, and whether you use streaming or non-streaming responses? Also whether you have client-side retries/backoff configured.

Jordan (Acme): prompts ~80 tokens, max_tokens=256, mostly streaming, spikes from 50 -> 800 rps over <30s. No retries during the spike.

Maria S (sre): that spike is likely tripping the per-key token/sec quota or the per-instance burst control. We throttle to protect other tenants and the customer’s own SLA. Because you don't retry, many clients get immediate 429 instead of smoothing.

Sanjay P (eng): two-pronged troubleshooting steps:
1) Check the per-key quota counters in Console -> Usage -> Per-key quota (we can confirm token/sec limits and any recent quota resets).
2) Capture server-side request_id for a 429 and forward to infra team — we can trace whether it's a quota tree or an instance-level circuit breaker.

Alex G (support): Jordan — if you can reproduce, run a quick curl with headers and include --trace-ascii to show timing. Example we asked for:

```
curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate \
  -d '{"prompt":"hello","max_tokens":256,"stream":true}' --trace-ascii -
```

Jordan (Acme): attached trace shows the request was accepted by ded-42, then queued ~120ms before streaming started. Many of the 429s have reset values of ~30–200s.

Maria S (sre): reset=30–200s is consistent with quota-window exhaustion, not just batching. We should check if customer-level monthly/commit quotas (token budget) are exhausted or if they hit a short-term burst quota (tokens/sec). BillingBot — can you confirm Acme's current committed capacity and quota windows?

BillingBot: AcmeApp (acct: acme-99) committed Dedicated: 8k tokens/sec sustained; burst allowed to 20k tokens/sec for 60s. Current 30-day usage at 87% of committed. Last 24h: short spike consumed ~35% of burst allowance.

Sanjay P (eng): that explains it — they hit burst allowance ceiling. After the burst allowance is depleted, the system enforces a cooldown and returns 429s with reset set to remaining cooldown seconds.

Alex G (support): recommended mitigations for now (short-term):
- Add client-side smoothing: exponential backoff + jitter and a small retry on 429 with Retry-After.
- Spread requests across multiple API keys if possible (dedicated per-key quotas independent).
- Lower max_tokens or split large prompts to reduce per-request token usage during spikes.

Sanjay P (eng): and for batching/latency:
- Tune batching window: set max_batch_latency_ms lower for latency-sensitive endpoints, or set batch_size caps per route. Example config snippet for Private/Dedicated runtime agent: 

```
serving:
  batching:
    enabled: true
    max_batch_latency_ms: 30
    max_batch_tokens: 1024
    max_requests_per_batch: 32
```

- Enable KV cache warmup for hot prefixes and set kv_cache.ttl_ms sufficiently long. Example: `kv_cache:{enabled:true,ttl_ms:86400000}`

Maria S (sre): operational fixes we can do:
- We can temporarily raise Acme's burst window (ops change) for the next 2 hours while they finish load testing.
- Add a canary route with smaller batch latency for their critical endpoints so they avoid being batched with large offline workloads.

Alex G (support): next steps — Jordan, do you want us to: 1) temporarily raise burst quota, 2) create a low-latency canary route, 3) provide client config examples? Please pick which you want.

Jordan (Acme): please 1 and 3. We'll also implement retry+backoff on our side. Thanks.

InfraOpsBot: created ticket INF-1412 to increase acme-99 burst allowance to 40k tokens/sec for 2 hours; note: change will take ~3–5 minutes to propagate.

Maria S (sre): I'll also add a monitoring alert for: per-key token/sec >= 80% for >30s so we can proactively reach out next time.

Sanjay P (eng): FYI — follow-up item: we'll prioritize a small UX patch in Console to show remaining burst allowance and exact cooldown time per key. Filing ENG-872.

Alex G (support): thanks everyone. Jordan — let us know after the next run and paste a failing x-request-id if you still see 429s or long batch delays.

Jordan (Acme): will do — re-running in ~10m. Appreciate the quick turnaround! :thumbsup:
